notes.meaning: Moses warned the people to step back from the tents of these rebellious men and not to touch any of their belongings. Because the rebels had defied God, everything they owned was devoted to destruction. If the people lingered or took anything, they would share in the same punishment. God called His people to separate themselves completely from evil.

The congregation obeyed the warning and backed away from the tents of the rebels. Dathan and Abiram then walked outside and stood boldly in their tent doorways with their wives, children, and infants. Instead of humbling themselves and asking for mercy, they showed open defiance against God and Moses.

Moses told the assembly how they would know that God had truly appointed him and that he was not acting on his own authority. If these rebels died of old age, illness, or any ordinary human disaster, it would mean the Lord had not sent him. But if God created something entirely new by causing the ground to split open and swallow them alive into the place of the dead, it would prove they had treated the Lord with contempt.

As soon as Moses stopped speaking, the ground cracked open beneath the feet of the rebels. The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, their families, their servants, and all their goods, and then it closed right back over them. They vanished alive into the pit in an instant, showing God's complete and terrifying judgment against their rebellion.

When the surrounding Israelites heard the desperate screams of the sinking families, they ran away in terror. They panicked and worried that the ground might split open and swallow them as well. Their sudden flight came from sheer fear and a guilty conscience rather than true repentance.

At the tabernacle, fire shot out from the presence of the Lord and instantly burned up the two hundred and fifty men who were offering incense. These men had tried to take on the holy duties of the priesthood for themselves. God showed that He is a consuming fire and will not allow unauthorized worship.

The Lord ordered Moses to have Eleazar the priest collect the bronze incense burners from among the charred bodies. The coals were to be dumped far away, but the bronze pans themselves were holy because they had been presented before God. Eleazar was to hammer them into flat sheets to cover the altar of sacrifice, creating a visible warning of what happened to those who sinned at the cost of their own lives.

Eleazar followed the command and had the bronze pans hammered into metal plates to overlay the altar. This new covering served as a lasting sign to remind Israel never to allow anyone outside Aaron's family to burn incense before the Lord. It stood as a permanent warning so that no one else would bring about the same terrible fate as Korah.

The very next morning, the entire community began complaining against Moses and Aaron, accusing them of murdering God's people. In their stubbornness, they called the punished rebels the Lord's people and blamed their leaders for God's direct judgment. This shocking reaction showed how blind and hardened the human heart can become even after seeing God's power.

As the angry crowd mobbed Moses and Aaron, the two leaders turned toward the Tent of Meeting for help and refuge. Suddenly the dark cloud covered the tent, and the bright, glorious presence of the Lord broke through. Moses and Aaron then stepped to the front of the tent to hear what God would say.

The Lord told Moses and Aaron to step away from the crowd so He could wipe out the rebels in a single moment. Instead of running to save themselves, both leaders immediately fell facedown on the ground in prayer. They chose to beg God for mercy rather than rejoice over the destruction of their enemies.

Moses realized that God's judgment had already broken out, so he commanded Aaron to act immediately. He told Aaron to put live coals from the altar and incense into his pan and run out into the camp to make atonement, which means to turn away God's wrath and restore peace. The deadly plague was spreading rapidly, and only the high priest's ministry could stop it.

Aaron took the incense burner and ran straight into the crowd, where people were falling dead all around him. He offered the holy incense and stood directly between the dead and the living until the deadly plague halted. In putting his own life on the line to rescue a rebellious people, Aaron served as a picture of Jesus Christ, our great High Priest who steps in to save dying sinners.

The sudden plague killed fourteen thousand seven hundred people in just a short time, besides those who had died the day before with Korah. The terrible death toll showed that rebelling against God brings severe judgment. God's holiness cannot be treated lightly by those He has called to be His people.

Once the plague had completely stopped, Aaron walked back to join Moses at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The work of intercession had succeeded, and the remaining people were spared. This confirmed beyond any doubt that Aaron was truly God's appointed high priest who brought life rather than death.
